subject: foundations
title: Field extensions and minimal polynomials
summary: Minimal polynomials define fields generated by roots. Extension degrees, embeddings, and separability explain how these fields fit together.
questionsAnswered: Why does an irreducible polynomial define a field?
How are minimal polynomials and extension degrees related?
When does a field generated by one root contain all the roots?
When does irreducibility survive an extension of the ground field?

sections.title: Minimal polynomials
sections.body:
Let \(E/K\) be a field extension and let \(\alpha\in E\) be algebraic over \(K\). Among the nonzero polynomials in \(K[x]\) that vanish at \(\alpha\), choose a monic one of least degree. This is the minimal polynomial \(m_{\alpha,K}\).

It is irreducible: a factorization into positive degrees would force one factor to vanish at \(\alpha\), contradicting minimality. The division algorithm also shows that every polynomial vanishing at \(\alpha\) is divisible by \(m_{\alpha,K}\). These properties prove uniqueness.

For example, \(x^2-2\) is the minimal polynomial of \(\sqrt2\) over \(\mathbb Q\). The polynomial \(x^4-4\) also vanishes at \(\sqrt2\), but it is not minimal:

\[x^4-4=(x^2-2)(x^2+2).\]

Over \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\), the minimal polynomial is instead \(x-\sqrt2\). The coefficient field is part of the definition.

sections.title: Arithmetic modulo an irreducible polynomial
sections.body:
Theorem

For a field \(K\) and a nonconstant polynomial \(m\in K[x]\), the quotient \(K[x]/(m)\) is a field if and only if \(m\) is irreducible. If \(m\) is monic of degree \(n\), this field has basis \(1,\alpha,\ldots,\alpha^{n-1}\), where \(\alpha\) is the class of \(x\).

Proof

When \(m\) is irreducible, a nonzero class has a representative \(g\) of degree less than \(n\) with \(\gcd(g,m)=1\). Bézout’s identity gives \(ug+vm=1\), so the class of \(u\) is its inverse. Conversely, if \(m=gh\) with both degrees positive, the nonzero classes of \(g,h\) multiply to zero; the quotient cannot be a field. The basis assertion follows from division with remainder.

Evaluation at an algebraic element gives an isomorphism \(K[x]/(m_{\alpha,K})\cong K(\alpha)\). Thus

\[[K(\alpha):K]=\deg m_{\alpha,K}.\]

Example

In \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\), with \(\alpha^3=2\), multiplication reduces using this relation. In particular,

\[(\alpha+1)(\alpha^2-\alpha+1)=\alpha^3+1=3,\qquad (\alpha+1)^{-1}=\frac{\alpha^2-\alpha+1}{3}.\]

citations.locator: 1.25 and the discussion of stem fields, pp. 14–16

sections.title: The tower law
sections.body:
Theorem

For finite extensions \(K\subseteq E\subseteq L\),

\[[L:K]=[L:E]\,[E:K].\]

If \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\) is a basis of \(E/K\) and \(u_1,\ldots,u_s\) is a basis of \(L/E\), then the \(rs\) products \(e_i u_j\) form a basis of \(L/K\). This proves the formula and shows how to construct a basis through successive adjunctions.

Example

Set \(L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt[3]3)\). Its degree is at most \(2\cdot3=6\). Since it contains subfields of degrees two and three, the tower law shows that both two and three divide \([L:\mathbb Q]\). Hence \([L:\mathbb Q]=6\). The six elements \(1,\sqrt[3]3,\sqrt[3]9,\sqrt2,\sqrt2\sqrt[3]3,\sqrt2\sqrt[3]9\) are a basis.

In particular, the degree of every intermediate field divides the degree of the full extension. A prime-degree extension therefore has no proper intermediate field.

sections.title: Roots and embeddings
sections.body:
A \(K\)-embedding \(K(\alpha)\to\overline K\) is determined by the image of \(\alpha\), which must be a root of \(m_{\alpha,K}\). Conversely, every root of this polynomial gives such an embedding. Thus the number of embeddings equals the number of distinct roots of the minimal polynomial.

An element is separable when its minimal polynomial has distinct roots. A finite extension \(E/K\) is separable when every element of \(E\) is separable over \(K\); equivalently, it has exactly \([E:K]\) embeddings into \(\overline K\). In characteristic zero, all finite extensions are separable.

An embedding need not be an automorphism of the original field. The three embeddings of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)\) into \(\mathbb C\) send \(\sqrt[3]2\) to its three conjugate roots. Only the real root lies in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)\), so this field has no nonidentity \(\mathbb Q\)-automorphism.

sections.title: Splitting fields and normality
sections.body:
A splitting field of \(f\in K[x]\) is an extension generated over \(K\) by all roots of \(f\). It exists by adjoining roots successively, and any two splitting fields are isomorphic over \(K\). An algebraic extension \(L/K\) is normal when every irreducible polynomial in \(K[x]\) having a root in \(L\) splits completely there. A finite extension is normal exactly when it is the splitting field of some polynomial.

A finite extension is Galois when it is both normal and separable. Its automorphism group has order \([L:K]\). In particular, the splitting field of a separable polynomial is Galois. For a degree-\(n\) separable polynomial, the faithful action on its roots embeds this group in \(S_n\), so the splitting-field degree divides \(n!\).

Example · \(x^4-2\)

Let \(\alpha=2^{1/4}>0\). Eisenstein gives \([\mathbb Q(\alpha):\mathbb Q]=4\). The splitting field is \(L=\mathbb Q(\alpha,i)\), and \([L:\mathbb Q]=8\) because \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\) is real. The automorphisms

\[r(\alpha)=i\alpha,\quad r(i)=i,\qquad s(\alpha)=\alpha,\quad s(i)=-i\]

satisfy \(r^4=s^2=1\) and \(srs=r^{-1}\). They generate the dihedral group of order eight, acting on the four roots as the symmetries of a square.

citations.note: The splitting field and dihedral group of x⁴−2.

sections.title: Characteristic and separability
sections.body:
For an irreducible polynomial \(m\), a repeated root occurs exactly when \(m'=0\). Indeed, \(\gcd(m,m')\ne1\) would force \(m\mid m'\), which is possible only when the derivative vanishes. In characteristic \(p\), this means that every exponent with a nonzero coefficient is divisible by \(p\).

Over a finite field, the map \(a\mapsto a^p\) is bijective. If an irreducible polynomial of degree greater than one had zero derivative, taking \(p\)-th roots of its coefficients would express it as a \(p\)-th power, a contradiction. This proves that finite fields are perfect.

The field \(\mathbb F_p(t)\) is not perfect: \(t\) is not a \(p\)-th power there. The polynomial \(x^p-t\) is Eisenstein at \(t\) in \(\mathbb F_p[t][x]\), hence irreducible over \(\mathbb F_p(t)\). Its derivative is zero, and it has only one distinct root. This is why irreducibility alone does not ensure a transitive action on as many distinct roots as the degree.

citations.note: Gauss’s lemma over a unique factorization domain.

sections.title: A single generator
sections.body:
The primitive element theorem states that every finite separable extension has the form \(K(\theta)\) for one element \(\theta\). For an infinite ground field, a useful form says that if \(K(\alpha,\beta)/K\) is finite and separable, then \(\theta=\alpha+c\beta\) generates the extension for all but finitely many \(c\in K\). The exceptional choices occur when two distinct embeddings have the same value on \(\alpha+c\beta\).

Example

Take \(\theta=\sqrt2+\sqrt3\). Since \(\theta^{-1}=\sqrt3-\sqrt2\),

\[\sqrt2=\frac{\theta-\theta^{-1}}2,\qquad \sqrt3=\frac{\theta+\theta^{-1}}2.\]

Consequently \(\mathbb Q(\theta)=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)\), an extension of degree four. Squaring gives \(\theta^2=5+2\sqrt6\), and therefore

\[\theta^4-10\theta^2+1=0.\]

The degree calculation proves that \(x^4-10x^2+1\) is its minimal polynomial and is irreducible. This field already contains the four roots \(\pm\sqrt2\pm\sqrt3\), so it is also the splitting field.

citations.note: The quartic example and its roots.

sections.title: Trace and norm
sections.body:
For a finite extension \(E/K\), multiplication by \(u\in E\) is a \(K\)-linear map on \(E\). Its trace and determinant are the field trace \(\operatorname{Tr}_{E/K}(u)\) and field norm \(N_{E/K}(u)\). The norm is multiplicative because determinants are multiplicative.

For a separable extension, these quantities are the sum and product of \(\sigma(u)\) over all \(K\)-embeddings \(\sigma:E\to\overline K\). In particular, if \(E=K(\alpha)\) and the minimal polynomial is \(m(x)=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0\), then

\[\operatorname{Tr}_{E/K}(\alpha)=-a_{n-1},\qquad N_{E/K}(\alpha)=(-1)^n a_0,\qquad N_{E/K}(\alpha-c)=(-1)^n m(c)\quad(c\in K).\]

Example

In \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\), the norm of \(a+b\sqrt2\) is \(a^2-2b^2\). Thus \(N(1+\sqrt2)=-1\). Since a square has square norm, \(1+\sqrt2\) is not a square in this field. This gives an irreducibility test for \(x^2-(1+\sqrt2)\).

Norms therefore detect some power obstructions in Capelli’s composition theorem. They also connect irreducibility with discriminants: for a monic separable irreducible polynomial \(f\) of degree \(n\) and a root \(\alpha\),

\[\operatorname{disc}(f)=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}N_{K(\alpha)/K}(f'(\alpha)).\]

The product formula for the norm turns this into the usual product of squared root differences.

citations.locator: Proposition 5.44, Corollary 5.45, Remark 5.47, and Proposition 5.49, pp. 106–108

sections.title: Irreducibility after extending the ground field
sections.body:
Proposition

Let \(f\in K[x]\) be irreducible of degree \(n\), and let \(E/K\) be a finite extension of degree \(m\). If \(\gcd(n,m)=1\), then \(f\) remains irreducible over \(E\).

Proof

Choose a root \(\alpha\) of \(f\) in an algebraic closure containing \(E\), and put \(d=[E(\alpha):E]\). The two towers give

\[md=[E(\alpha):K]=n[E(\alpha):K(\alpha)].\]

Thus \(n\mid md\). Coprimality gives \(n\mid d\), while \(d\le n\) because \(f(\alpha)=0\). Hence \(d=n\), which is the required irreducibility.

For example, an irreducible cubic over \(\mathbb Q\) remains irreducible over every quadratic extension. Its Galois group can nevertheless change: adjoining a primitive cube root of unity changes the group of \(x^3-2\) from \(S_3\) to \(C_3\). More generally, the intersection with the splitting field determines the new group.

citations.note: The displayed consequence is proved directly by the tower law.
Galois groups after extending the coefficient field.

subject: foundations
title: The Galois correspondence and intermediate fields
summary: Subgroups describe intermediate fields, changes of ground field, and blocks in the action on roots. Examples show how to use the correspondence in group calculations.
questionsAnswered: Which subgroup corresponds to the field generated by one root?
How do intermediate fields determine whether a root action is primitive?
When is the Galois group of a compositum a direct product?
How does extending the ground field change the Galois group?

sections.title: Fixed fields
sections.body:
Let \(L/K\) be a finite Galois extension and let \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\). For a subgroup \(H\le G\), define

\[L^H=\{a\in L:\sigma(a)=a\text{ for every }\sigma\in H\}.\]

This is a field containing \(K\). Requiring more automorphisms to fix an element gives a smaller field: if \(H_1\subseteq H_2\), then \(L^{H_2}\subseteq L^{H_1}\). In the other direction, an intermediate field \(E\) gives the subgroup \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)\).

Fundamental theorem of Galois theory

These two constructions are inverse bijections. If \(E=L^H\), then

\[[L:E]=|H|,\qquad [E:K]=[G:H].\]

Moreover, \(E/K\) is Galois if and only if \(H\) is normal in \(G\). In that case restriction induces \(\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)\cong G/H\).

The theorem depends on both normality and separability. For example, \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)/\mathbb Q\) has degree three but trivial automorphism group; its automorphisms do not recover the ground field as their fixed field.

sections.title: A root field and its stabilizer
sections.body:
Suppose \(L\) is the splitting field of a separable irreducible polynomial \(f\in K[x]\), and let \(\alpha\) be a root. Its stabilizer is

\[H=G_\alpha=\{\sigma\in G:\sigma(\alpha)=\alpha\}=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(\alpha)).\]

The correspondence gives \(L^H=K(\alpha)\). The roots of \(f\) can be identified with the left cosets \(G/H\), by \(\sigma H\mapsto\sigma(\alpha)\). Therefore

\[\deg f=[K(\alpha):K]=[G:H],\qquad [L:K]=|G|.\]

For \(x^3-2\), the group is \(S_3\), and the stabilizer of the real root is generated by complex conjugation. Its order is two; its fixed field has degree three. The field generated by one root is thus represented by a stabilizer, while the whole splitting field is represented by the identity subgroup.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · a biquadratic extension

Let \(L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)\). Its four automorphisms independently change the signs of \(\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt3\), so \(G\cong C_2\times C_2\). Write \(s\) for the sign change of \(\sqrt2\), and \(t\) for that of \(\sqrt3\). The three subgroups of order two give exactly three quadratic subfields:

\[L^{\langle s\rangle}=\mathbb Q(\sqrt3),\quad L^{\langle t\rangle}=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2),\quad L^{\langle st\rangle}=\mathbb Q(\sqrt6).\]

The element \(\theta=\sqrt2+\sqrt3\) generates \(L\). Its minimal polynomial is \(x^4-10x^2+1\), with roots \(\pm\sqrt2\pm\sqrt3\). Each nonidentity automorphism exchanges two pairs of roots. The action is transitive, but contains neither a single transposition nor a 4-cycle.

All three subgroups are normal, so all three quadratic extensions are Galois. The correspondence also proves that there are no other proper intermediate fields.

sections.title: Intermediate fields and blocks
sections.body:
In a transitive action of \(G\) on a finite set \(\Omega\), a block is a nonempty subset \(B\) such that every translate \(\sigma B\) either equals \(B\) or is disjoint from \(B\). The action is primitive if its only blocks are singletons and \(\Omega\).

For the action on the roots of \(f\), let \(H=G_\alpha\). Subgroups \(H\subseteq U\subseteq G\) correspond to blocks containing \(\alpha\), by \(U\mapsto U\alpha\). Under the coset description \(\Omega\cong G/H\), these are the subsets \(U/H\); their translates partition \(G/H\). Conversely, the setwise stabilizer of a block containing \(\alpha\) is such a subgroup and acts transitively on that block.

Proposition

The action of \(G\) on the roots of a separable irreducible polynomial is primitive if and only if the extension \(K(\alpha)/K\) has no proper intermediate field.

Indeed, a proper block corresponds to \(H\subsetneq U\subsetneq G\), hence to \(K\subsetneq L^U\subsetneq K(\alpha)\). This proves at once that irreducible polynomials of prime degree have primitive Galois action. Composite degree does not rule out primitivity; the question is whether intermediate fields actually exist.

For the biquadratic example, fixing \(\sqrt2\) partitions the roots into \(\{\sqrt2+\sqrt3,\sqrt2-\sqrt3\}\) and its negative. These two blocks reflect the intermediate field \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\).

citations.note: The field formulation follows by the Galois correspondence.

sections.title: Composita and intersections
sections.body:
Let \(L_1/K\) and \(L_2/K\) be finite Galois extensions in a common algebraic closure. Their compositum \(L_1L_2\) is the field generated by both. An automorphism of this field is determined by its restrictions to \(L_1\) and \(L_2\), and the restrictions must agree on the intersection.

Theorem

Restriction identifies \(\operatorname{Gal}(L_1L_2/K)\) with

\[\{(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\in\operatorname{Gal}(L_1/K)\times\operatorname{Gal}(L_2/K):\sigma_1|_{L_1\cap L_2}=\sigma_2|_{L_1\cap L_2}\}.\]

In particular, it is the full direct product if and only if \(L_1\cap L_2=K\). Equivalently, in this case \([L_1L_2:K]=[L_1:K][L_2:K]\).

For \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\) and \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)\), the intersection is \(\mathbb Q\), giving the group \(C_2\times C_2\) above. For larger splitting fields, determining their intersection is often the main step in a group computation. The Galois hypothesis is essential to the stated intersection criterion.

citations.note: Compatible pairs, direct products, and the need for the Galois hypothesis.

sections.title: Changing the ground field
sections.body:
Let \(f\in K[x]\) be separable, let \(L\) be its splitting field, and let \(E/K\) be a finite extension in the same algebraic closure. The splitting field over \(E\) is \(LE\). Restriction gives

\[\operatorname{Gal}(LE/E)\cong\operatorname{Gal}(L/L\cap E)\le\operatorname{Gal}(L/K).\]

Thus an extension of the ground field replaces the original group by the subgroup fixing \(L\cap E\). The polynomial remains irreducible over \(E\) exactly when this subgroup is transitive on the roots. If \(L\cap E=K\), the whole permutation group is unchanged.

For \(f=x^3-2\), adjoining a primitive cube root of unity replaces \(S_3\) by \(A_3\cong C_3\), which is still transitive. Adjoining the real cube root replaces \(S_3\) by its order-two stabilizer, which fixes one root. In the first case the polynomial remains irreducible; in the second it factors.

The intersection formula concerns a Galois splitting field \(L\). It should not be replaced by an intersection calculation with only one root field.

sections.title: Elements fixed by a subgroup
sections.body:
For any \(u\in L\), the distinct values \(\sigma(u)\), with \(\sigma\in G\), are the roots of its minimal polynomial over \(K\). Consequently

\[m_{u,K}(T)=\prod_{v\in G\cdot u}(T-v),\qquad [K(u):K]=[G:G_u].\]

This gives a general way to find subfields: choose an expression in the roots whose stabilizer is known. The coefficients of the orbit polynomial lie in \(K\), because every element of \(G\) permutes its factors. Resolvent constructions use such expressions to test which subgroup can contain the Galois group.

The discriminant is the simplest example. Assume \(\operatorname{char}K\ne2\), write \(f=a_n\prod_i(x-\alpha_i)\), and put

\[\delta=a_n^{n-1}\prod_{iA permutation of the roots multiplies \(\delta\) by its sign. Hence \(G\subseteq A_n\) if and only if \(\Delta(f)\) is a square in \(K\). If it is not a square, \(K(\delta)\) is the quadratic field fixed by \(G\cap A_n\). This describes a quadratic subfield; it does not determine the whole group.

sections.title: Applications
sections.body:
These correspondences explain several recurring methods. Intermediate fields reveal blocks and therefore possible imprimitive groups. Intersections determine groups of composita. Adjoining constants changes the arithmetic group to a subgroup, an essential step when comparing arithmetic and geometric Galois groups. Invariant expressions produce resolvents and distinguished subfields.

For polynomial composition, Capelli’s theorem asks whether the inner polynomial minus a root of the outer one is irreducible over that root field. For iterates, the successive equations build towers of fields, and their Galois groups act on the corresponding tree of preimages. The same field-theoretic ideas therefore continue beyond a single action on finitely many roots.
